title: Leeches: Oh Hell No!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore leeches: their body biology (segments, suckers, ganglia and the 'thirty-two brains' myth), land leeches, the three feeding categories (jawed, jawless, worm leeches), saliva compounds like hirudin that thin blood and act as vasodilators, the Tyrant king leech (Haementeria/Tyrant king leech in the Amazon) that enters nasal and other body cavities, the Napoleon's soldiers in Egypt case, hermaphroditic reproduction and cocoons, kangaroo leech, and how to safely remove one. Second half covers bloodletting under the humoral theory, Dr. François Broussais and leech mania in early nineteenth-century Europe, leech gatherers, the revival through reconstructive surgery (Dr. Joseph Upton and the Boston boy's ear case), the FDA's 2004 approval of medical leeches, and leech therapy clinics. Episode ends with listener mail correcting French pronunciation of 'foie gras' and a plug for a family member's film.

segments.title: Opening banter and leech plans
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the leeches episode as a follow-up to the dentistry episode on medical leeches, and discuss the earthworm connection.

segments.title: Leech body anatomy and the thirty-two brains myth
segments.summary: Leeches are ringed with 32 segments and have front and rear suckers. The hosts debunk the claim of thirty-two brains: they have two brains plus ganglia, about 21 ganglia total. Land leeches are discussed as ticks-like bloodsuckers that detect CO2.

segments.title: Leech feeding types and jawed leeches
segments.summary: There are about 600-700 leech species in three feeding categories: sanguivorous, worm leeches, and others. Jawed leeches have denticles that saw into skin and create suction; the myth that leech saliva contains an anesthetic is debunked.

segments.title: Jawless leeches and the Amazon giant leech
segments.summary: Jawless leeches include the giant Amazon leech, which can grow very long and uses a proboscis like a hypodermic needle to draw blood. The hosts discuss whether denticles or proboscis is worse.

segments.title: Break and host banter
segments.summary: Mid-episode break followed by casual banter about a guest producer list and a family member's upcoming film release.

segments.title: Leech eyesight, saliva compounds, and feeding
segments.summary: Leech eyesight varies with age and vibration sensing via body hairs. Leech saliva contains anticoagulant and vasodilator compounds, and leeches can feed up to ten times body weight and go months between meals.

segments.title: Tyrant king leech and internal infestations
segments.summary: The tyrant king leech in the Amazon can enter nasal cavities, eyes, urethra and other body openings and stay for weeks or months. A 1930s-era case describes a girl whose leg was infested by a leech moving within her body, and Napoleon's soldiers in Egypt in 1798 died after leeches blocked airways via drinking water.

segments.title: Leech reproduction and kangaroo leech
segments.summary: Leeches are hermaphroditic and exchange sperm via a spermatophore, producing hardy cocoons from the clitellum. The kangaroo leech carries young in a pouch and shoots them onto frogs.

segments.title: Removing a leech safely
segments.summary: Advice on removing a leech: do not panic, do not squeeze or use salt or alcohol because it may cause vomiting and infection; gently break the seal with a fingernail or card, flick it off, and clean and dress the bleeding wound.

segments.title: Bloodletting history and leech mania
segments.summary: Bloodletting was based on humoral theory. Early nineteenth-century Europe saw leech mania; Dr. François Broussais used leeches widely and fell from favor after a cholera epidemic in 1832. Leech gatherers waded into water to collect leeches.

segments.title: Revival of medical leeches in surgery
segments.summary: Leeches were revived in reconstructive surgery. Dr. Joseph Upton used thirty leeches to save a Boston boy's reattached ear. The FDA approved medical leeches as a device in 2004, and leech therapy clinics make broader claims that the hosts caution against.

segments.title: Leech-themed anecdotes and wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the lawyer Thomas Erskine who kept leeches, a pet leech anecdote, and close out the leech topic.

segments.title: Listener mail: French pronunciation
segments.summary: Robin from Victoria, BC corrects the pronunciation of foie gras, noting the silent final letter and soft C rule, prompting the hosts to pledge to say it correctly.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to send lessons by email and sign off.
